strengths: Presents a well-motivated, unifying probabilistic framework (Product of Experts) that generalizes composition of heterogeneous generative and discriminative models (diffusion/flow models, autoregressive models, VLMs, physics simulators) at inference time, without retraining.

Provides a concrete and practical sampling algorithm (AIS + SMC with conditional generative expert composition) with clear derivations connecting flow-model score functions to the annealed sampling procedure.

Demonstrates broad applicability across diverse tasks: graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, and regionally composed text-to-image generation, showing the framework's flexibility for different input modalities (text, image, low-level pose/trajectory).
Includes an alternative autoregressive instantiation (Appendix C) showing the framework generalizes beyond flow-based diffusion models.
Provides ablation studies (e.g., conditional sampling, particle counts) that support specific design choices in the framework.
Combines both automatic quantitative metrics (LPIPS, MSE, VBench-style scores) and VLM-based (GPT-4o) evaluation across multiple perceptual dimensions (controllability, quality, alignment).
The intermediate sample visualizations (Fig. 8) offer useful insight into how the SMC resampling process improves alignment over iterations.
weaknesses: Evaluation datasets are quite small (e.g., 30 scenes for image editing, 12 scenes for physics-instructed video generation), limiting the statistical robustness of the reported metrics and their standard deviations.

Most experiments compose only 2 generative/discriminative experts, which is a fairly limited demonstration of the claimed generality of combining many heterogeneous knowledge sources; scalability to larger numbers of experts is not empirically shown.

Baselines are relatively narrow (single baseline per task: RF-Solver, monolithic Wan2.1 variants, PhysGen3D), and the paper does not compare against other SMC-based or compositional reward-steering methods cited in related work (e.g., [46, 55]), making it harder to assess relative advantages.

The key approximation used for annealed discriminative rewards (r_t(x) ≈ r(x̂)) and the conditional sampling update (Eq. 7) rely on heuristic justifications rather than rigorous theoretical analysis of bias or convergence guarantees.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o as an evaluation judge for multiple metrics raises reproducibility and potential bias concerns; no human evaluation is included despite central claims about improved 'user controllability.'
Computational overhead is substantial (up to ~30 minutes per video sample) but not directly benchmarked against baseline inference costs in terms of quality-per-compute tradeoffs.
Quantitative improvements in some settings (e.g., Table 2, physics-instructed video generation) are modest or mixed across metrics, weakening the strength of the controllability claims.
Limited discussion/empirical exploration of failure cases where experts are incompatible, despite this being noted as a core assumption/limitation of the method.

strengths: Presents a unifying probabilistic Product-of-Experts framework that can combine heterogeneous sources (diffusion/flow generative models, autoregressive models, VLM-based discriminative rewards, and physics-simulator-derived signals) at inference time without retraining, which is a conceptually appealing and practically useful contribution.

Technically sound sampling procedure combining Annealed Importance Sampling with per-timestep MCMC kernels and SMC-style resampling, explicitly contrasted with path-wise importance weighting used in concurrent work (Skreta et al. 2025, He et al. 2025) to avoid weight degeneracy.

Demonstrates the framework's versatility across three distinct and practically motivated applications: graphics-engine-instructed image object/character insertion, physics-simulator-instructed video generation (both flow-based and autoregressive), and layout-controlled text-to-image generation.

Reasonably thorough empirical comparisons against multiple relevant, recent, strong baselines (RF-Solver, Magic Insert, Add-it, FLUX-Fill, SDEdit, PhysGen3D, 3DIS-FLUX) using a mix of automated metrics (MSE, LPIPS, IoU, VQAScore) and GPT-4o-based evaluation.

Useful ablations isolating the effect of conditional sampling (Eq. 6) and particle count/SMC resampling, and a clear specification of practical instantiations for flow and autoregressive experts (Section 3.3, Appendix C).
weaknesses: Evaluation datasets are quite small in most tasks (e.g., 30, 80, 12, 9, and 50 scenes), limiting statistical robustness of the reported improvements and raising concerns about generalization to larger-scale or more diverse settings.

No human/user study is conducted to validate controllability or perceptual quality claims; the paper relies heavily on GPT-4o as an automatic judge, which can introduce its own biases and is not independently validated for this specific evaluation protocol.

Ablation results are mixed: Table 4 shows that removing SMC resampling sometimes yields comparable or even better mIoU, partially undercutting the claimed benefit of SMC, and the paper does not fully reconcile this tension.

The framework is only demonstrated with a small number of experts (2-3) per task; the paper's motivating claim of integrating "many heterogeneous" experts is not stress-tested at larger scale, leaving open questions about scalability and expert-conflict resolution as N grows.

Despite explicitly distinguishing the proposed method from concurrent works (Skreta et al. 2025; He et al. 2025) in the related work section, no direct empirical comparison against these closely related PoE/SMC-based diffusion composition methods is provided.

The conditional-expert approximation (Eq. 6/9) and the discriminative-expert endpoint approximation (Eq. 8) are heuristic simplifications without theoretical guarantees on sampling correctness or convergence, and their sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., weight w, number of MCMC/conditional steps) is not thoroughly analyzed.

Reported compute overhead is substantial (e.g., ~30 min per sample for autoregressive video composition), and while acknowledged as a limitation, the paper provides limited discussion of how this scales with more experts or higher resolutions/longer videos.
